matching.reasoningTemplate: Altered sensorium with hypothermia and bradycardia in a hypothyroid patient suggests myxoedema coma.

clinicalPearls: Myxedema coma carries a 20-40% mortality despite intensive care, and outcome does not correlate with the degree of T4 or TSH abnormality (p.3032).
It occurs almost exclusively in the elderly, often in winter, and may arise either in a known hypothyroid patient with poor treatment adherence or in someone not previously diagnosed (p.3032).
Hypothermia in myxedema can be profound, reaching as low as 23 degrees C (74 degrees F) (p.3032).
Reduced consciousness is the hallmark and may be accompanied by seizures, alongside the usual signs of hypothyroidism (p.3032).
A distinguishing examination clue in hypothyroidism is a deep tendon reflex (e.g., Achilles) whose relaxation phase is prolonged out of proportion to the contraction phase (p.3769).
Hypothyroidism, especially extreme as in myxedema coma, is a recognised endocrine cause of hypothermia by reducing metabolic rate and impairing thermogenesis and behavioural responses (p.3768).

Bradycardia, reduced myocardial contractility and stroke volume, and pericardial effusion (up to ~30% of hypothyroid patients) reflect the cardiac depression that underlies the haemodynamic picture (p.3030).
Carotene accumulation can give the skin a yellow tinge, and nonpitting (myxedematous) tissue swelling distinguishes the oedema from pitting fluid overload (p.3029-3030).
harrison.pathophysiology: Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve in profound hypothyroidism, and impaired peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (p.3032; p.3768).
additionalDifferentials: Sick euthyroid syndrome confounding thyroid function tests in a critically ill or hypothermic patient (p.3769).
Adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism, which independently increase susceptibility to hypothermia and may coexist (p.3768).
Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030).
infectionMimics: Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769).
nonInfectiousMimics: Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768).
Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768).
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032).
Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769).
Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032).
redFlags: Reduced level of consciousness with seizures in a hypothyroid patient (p.3032).
Hypoventilation with hypoxia/hypercapnia signalling impending respiratory failure (p.3032).
An identifiable precipitant such as infection, MI, CHF, GI bleeding, cerebrovascular accident, or respiratory-depressant drugs (p.3032).
harrison.prognosis: Mortality remains 20-40% even with intensive treatment, and prognosis is independent of the measured T4 and TSH levels. Hypothermia associated with concurrent sepsis is a poor prognostic sign (p.3032, p.3769).
pitfalls: Sedatives, anesthetics, and antidepressants can precipitate or worsen myxedema coma, and impaired drug metabolism means standard doses may accumulate (p.3032).
Hypothermia masks fever and leukocytosis, so infection can be missed; rigors may be misread as shivering (p.3769).
Giving parenteral levothyroxine to a euthyroid hypothermic patient is potentially hazardous, so clinical/historical evidence of hypothyroidism should be sought first (p.3769).
Sick euthyroid syndrome can confound thyroid function tests in the acutely ill patient (p.3769).
